question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{-2/7}$ and that ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$ Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{2}{7}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-2/7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-2/7+1}}{(-\frac{2}{7}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/7}}{(\frac{5}{7})}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{5}{x}^{5/7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: What is the antiderivative of $\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}?$ Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}={x}^{-6}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-6$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{-6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-6+1}}{-6+1}+C \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{-5}}{5}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{5{x}^{5}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
